body.statement: Fix \(0<\alpha<1\) and a finite vector \(Q=(C_1(p),\ldots,C_d(p))\) returned by \(\mathsf{SC\mbox{-}CTFID}\).  Then \(\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{r,i}\varphi_r(X_{ri})+o_P(1)\) and converges to \(N(0,\Sigma_Q)\), possibly singular, and the plug-in covariance is consistent.  Let \(I_0=\{j:\Sigma_{Q,jj}>0\}\).  Under the thresholded definition of \(\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}\), \(P(\widehat I_+=I_0)\to1\); if \(I_0\ne\varnothing\), the Gaussian max-statistic region has limiting simultaneous coverage \(1-\alpha\) on \(I_0\).  Symbolically constant coordinates are exact equalities, and every other coordinate with zero first-order variance is reported as degenerate rather than studentized.
body.justification: For every returned regular circuit, automatic differentiation now yields a proved multi-regime influence function, singular covariance limit, consistent covariance estimate, and valid thresholded simultaneous region.
body.gap: The proof supplies the previously implicit threshold requirement by deriving \(O_P(\delta_n)=o_P(\kappa_n)\) matrix error from multinomial sampling and the circuit margin.
body.consumer: cfid can report estimates, influence functions, joint covariance, simultaneous intervals for positive-variance coordinates, exact symbolic cells, and separate first-order-degeneracy statuses.
body.proof_tex:
By \(\text{thm:sc-ctfid-output-soundness}\), every returned circuit used here is a rational function of the supplied regime probabilities on its verified domain.  Let \(m_r\) be the finite number of cells in regime \(r\), regard \(p_r\) and \(\widehat p_r\) as vectors in \(\mathbb R^{m_r}\), and concatenate the regime blocks.  By \(\text{ass:circuit-margin}\), every one of the finitely many circuit divisors has absolute value at least \(\varepsilon\) at \(p\).  Continuity gives an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(p\) on which all those divisors have absolute value at least \(\varepsilon/2\).  Each \(C_j\) is therefore twice continuously differentiable on \(U\); after shrinking \(U\) to a bounded neighborhood, the finitely many first and second derivatives are bounded there.

Write \(a_n=\max_{r\in\mathcal R}|n_r/n-\rho_r|\), so that \(\delta_n=n^{-1/2}+a_n\).  By \(\text{ass:positive-regime-fractions}\), there is \(c>0\) such that \(n_r/n\ge c\) for all regimes and all sufficiently large \(n\).  Under \(\text{ass:independent-regime-sampling}\),
\[
E\lVert\widehat p-p\rVert^2
=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\frac{1-\lVert p_r\rVert^2}{n_r}
\le \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\frac{1}{n_r}
=O(n^{-1}).
\]
Consequently \(\widehat p-p=O_P(n^{-1/2})\) and \(P(\widehat p\in U)\to1\).  Taylor expansion on this event, with the bounded Hessian just established, gives
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q)
=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}J_{Q,r}(p)\sqrt n(\widehat p_r-p_r)+o_P(1).
\]
For each fixed regime,
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat p_r-p_r)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n_r}\frac{n}{n_r}(e_{X_{ri}}-p_r).
\]
Because \(n/n_r\to\rho_r^{-1}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_r}(e_{X_{ri}}-p_r)=O_P(1)\), replacing \(n/n_r\) by \(\rho_r^{-1}\) changes the display by \(o_P(1)\).  There are only finitely many regimes.  Substitution therefore proves the asserted asymptotic linear representation
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\sum_{i=1}^{n_r}
\rho_r^{-1}J_{Q,r}(p)(e_{X_{ri}}-p_r)+o_P(1)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{r,i}\varphi_r(X_{ri})+o_P(1).
\]

We verify the joint limit directly, including the singular case.  For any fixed \(b\in\mathbb R^d\), put
\[
Y_{ri}=b^{\mathsf T}\rho_r^{-1}J_{Q,r}(p)(e_{X_{ri}}-p_r).
\]
These variables are independent and centered, and, because every alphabet and the regime menu are fixed, they are uniformly bounded.  Uniform third-order expansion yields
\[
E\exp\{itY_{ri}/\sqrt n\}
=1-\frac{t^2E(Y_{ri}^2)}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}),
\]
where the remainder is uniform in \(r,i\).  Summing the logarithms over \(\sum_r n_r=n\) observations gives
\[
\log E\exp\!\left\{\frac{it}{\sqrt n}\sum_{r,i}Y_{ri}\right\}
\longrightarrow -\frac{t^2}{2}\,b^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_Qb,
\]
because \(n_r/n\to\rho_r\) and
\[
\frac1n\sum_{r,i}E(Y_{ri}^2)
\longrightarrow
b^{\mathsf T}J_Q(p)\operatorname{blockdiag}_{r\in\mathcal R}
\left\{\rho_r^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(p_r)-p_rp_r^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\right\}
J_Q(p)^{\mathsf T}b.
\]
The right-hand side is \(b^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_Qb\).  Fourier inversion after convolution with an arbitrarily small nonsingular Gaussian shows from the displayed characteristic-function convergence that every contrast converges to its centered Gaussian law; letting the convolution variance decrease to zero gives the possibly degenerate limit.  Applying this simultaneously to the joint characteristic function proves
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat Q-Q)\ \rightsquigarrow\ N(0,\Sigma_Q).
\]

It remains to justify covariance estimation and the random threshold.  On \(U\), bounded second derivatives imply
\[
\lVert J_Q(\widehat p)-J_Q(p)\rVert=O_P(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The map \(u\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(u)-uu^{\mathsf T}\) is Lipschitz on each finite simplex.  Moreover, because both \(n_r/n\) and \(\rho_r\) are eventually bounded below by a positive constant,
\[
\left|\frac{n}{n_r}-\frac1{\rho_r}\right|
\le C\left|\frac{n_r}{n}-\rho_r\right|
\]
for one finite \(C\) and all sufficiently large \(n\).  Expanding the finite matrix products in the covariance formula therefore gives the coordinate-uniform bound
\[
\lVert\widehat\Sigma_Q-\Sigma_Q\rVert
=O_P(n^{-1/2}+a_n)=O_P(\delta_n).
\]
The threshold condition in \(\text{def:simultaneous-region}\) is explicit: \(\kappa_n\to0\) and \(\delta_n/\kappa_n\to0\).  Hence
\[
\lVert\widehat\Sigma_Q-\Sigma_Q\rVert=o_P(\kappa_n).
\]
Indeed, tightness of the preceding norm divided by \(\delta_n\), multiplied by the deterministic factor \(\delta_n/\kappa_n\to0\), proves the last display.  This supplies the covariance-estimation rate required by the threshold rather than assuming it.

Let \(I_0=\{j:\Sigma_{Q,jj}>0\}\).  If \(j\in I_0\), covariance consistency and \(\kappa_n\to0\) imply \(P(\widehat\Sigma_{Q,jj}>\kappa_n)\to1\).  If \(j\notin I_0\), positive semidefiniteness gives \(\widehat\Sigma_{Q,jj}\ge0\), and the \(o_P(\kappa_n)\) bound gives
\[
P\{\widehat\Sigma_{Q,jj}>\kappa_n\}
\le P\{\lVert\widehat\Sigma_Q-\Sigma_Q\rVert>\kappa_n\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Symbolically constant coordinates are excluded by definition and have zero diagonal variance.  A finite union bound over \(j=1,\ldots,d\) proves
\[
P(\widehat I_+=I_0)\longrightarrow1.
\]

Suppose \(I_0\ne\varnothing\).  On the event \(\widehat I_+=I_0\), covariance consistency implies convergence of the selected covariance matrix and of all its positive diagonal entries.  Couple the population and plug-in Gaussian vectors as \(Z=\Sigma_{Q,I_0,I_0}^{1/2}G\) and \(\widehat Z=\widehat\Sigma_{Q,I_0,I_0}^{1/2}G\) for one standard Gaussian \(G\).  Continuity of the positive-semidefinite square root gives \(\widehat Z\to Z\) in probability.  Therefore the plug-in law of
\[
\max_{j\in I_0}\frac{|\widehat Z_j|}{\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{Q,jj}}}
\]
converges to that of \(T=\max_{j\in I_0}|Z_j|/\sqrt{\Sigma_{Q,jj}}\).  The Gaussian law has a positive density on its linear support, and the boundary of each max-norm ball has Lebesgue measure zero in that support; hence \(T\) has a continuous distribution.  Scaling a nonzero support neighborhood also shows that its distribution function is strictly increasing on its nontrivial range.  Thus the plug-in \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile converges to the population quantile.  The joint Gaussian limit, Slutsky's argument for the consistent diagonal standardizers, and \(P(\widehat I_+=I_0)\to1\) now yield
\[
P\!\left(
|\widehat Q_j-Q_j|\le c_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{Q,jj}/n}
\text{ for every }j\in I_0
\right)\longrightarrow1-\alpha.
\]

If a circuit simplifies symbolically to a constant, its plug-in value equals that constant whenever the circuit is evaluated, so reporting it as an exact equality is valid.  Every other coordinate excluded with probability tending to one has \(\Sigma_{Q,jj}=0\); the proved selection result therefore justifies labeling it first-order degenerate and withholding a Wald interval.  This completes all claims, including consistency, singular Gaussian limits, threshold selection, and simultaneous coverage.
